passages.t: Job asks to be told the charge
passages.happening:
“I loathe my own life; I will express my complaint and speak in the bitterness of my soul” (verse 1).

“I will say to God: Do not condemn me! Let me know why You prosecute me” (verse 2). Does it please God to oppress him, to reject the work of his own hands and favor the schemes of the wicked?

“Do You have eyes of flesh? Do You see as man sees?” (verse 4). Are God's days short like a mortal's, that he must hunt for Job's sin and search it out, ‘though You know that I am not guilty, and there is no deliverance from Your hand?’ (verse 7).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 9 ended with Job's sense that he must face God alone. Chapter 10 is what he says once he decides to speak anyway. Nearly all of it is spoken to God.

Ancient courts took it for granted that an accused person had the right to know the charge. Job's request in verse 2 assumes that God, as a just judge, owes him at least a statement of the case.

His questions in verses 4 and 5 are bold. A human judge has to dig for evidence because he cannot see the heart and his time is short. God is not like that. So why, Job asks, does God act as though he must search Job out, when he already knows Job is not guilty?
passages.asks: Job asked God to tell him the charge. Ask whether you have ever felt accused without knowing why. And ask whether you would dare to ask God the question Job asked.

passages.happening:
Then the tender center of the chapter. “Your hands shaped me and altogether formed me. Would You now turn and destroy me? Please remember that You molded me like clay. Would You now return me to dust?” (verses 8-9).

“Did You not pour me out like milk, and curdle me like cheese? You clothed me with skin and flesh, and knit me together with bones and sinews. You have granted me life and loving devotion, and Your care has preserved my spirit” (verses 10-12).
passages.hearers:
Ancient people had no scientific account of how a child forms in the womb, and Job's pictures come from the kitchen and the loom. Milk poured out and curdled into cheese pictured conception and the first thickening of the body. Skin, flesh, bones and sinews knit together come from weaving, as if God made a body the way a skilled weaver made cloth, with care and intention.

Behind it stands Israel's picture in Genesis 2:7, where the LORD God forms the man from the dust. Clay, chomer, is the potter's material. Scripture often uses the image of God as potter to stress both his authority and his care. Job uses it to ask why the potter would smash his own work.

The word for loving devotion in verse 12 is chesed, love that keeps its commitments. Job names it as something God gave him. That is why God's apparent turn against him feels like betrayal.
passages.later: A psalm uses the same picture of God at work in the womb: “For You formed my inmost being; You knit me together in my mother’s womb” (Psalm 139:13). And Job's ‘return me to dust’ (verse 9) echoes the word to Adam: “For dust you are, and to dust you shall return” (Genesis 3:19).
passages.asks: Job remembered God's care even in his anguish. Ask what you know of God's care for you that you could hold on to on a dark day. And ask how it changes things to know that you were made with attention, not by accident.

passages.t: A hidden plan, and a land of darkness
passages.happening:
Then the memory turns to suspicion. “Yet You concealed these things in Your heart, and I know that this was in Your mind: If I sinned, You would take note, and would not acquit me of my iniquity” (verses 13-14). Guilty or righteous, Job cannot lift his head. If he did, God would hunt him like a lion.

“Why then did You bring me from the womb? Oh, that I had died, and no eye had seen me!” (verse 18). If only he had been carried from the womb to the grave.

“Are my days not few? Withdraw from me, that I may have a little comfort” (verse 20), before he goes, never to return, to a land of darkness and deep shadow, ‘where even the light is like darkness’ (verse 22).
passages.hearers:
The chapter traces a whole life, from the womb to the grave, spoken to the God who was present at both ends.

The land of darkness reflects the common Israelite picture of Sheol as a realm without light or order. The word for disorder in verse 22 means literally without order, and it suggests creation undone, where God had separated light from darkness and set everything in its place. Death, for Job, looks like creation run backward. Deep shadow, tsalmavet, is again the word of Psalm 23:4.
passages.later: A psalm of lament speaks of death in the same way, as a place where the light of God's works is not seen: “Will Your wonders be known in the darkness, or Your righteousness in the land of oblivion?” (Psalm 88:12).
passages.hard:
Job suggests that God made him only to watch him and hunt him down, and he wishes he had never been born. How should a reader take this?

In verses 13 to 17 Job wonders whether God's kindness in creating him was cover for a hidden intention to catch him in sin and destroy him. The reader knows from chapters 1 and 2 that this is not what is happening. God called Job blameless and set limits to his testing. So the chapter shows how suffering can distort what a person sees, making even memories of God's love look sinister.

Some interpreters stress that the book honors Job's willingness to speak these fears aloud to God rather than hide them. Others stress that the book later corrects them when God speaks from the whirlwind. Both are true to the text. The book's overall shape suggests that God is neither indifferent nor hostile, even when he seems so to the one who suffers. It does not pretend that the appearance is easy to bear.

Job's words about loathing his life (verse 1) and wishing he had never been born (verses 18-19) are recorded as a cry to God, not as counsel.

If you have thoughts of hurting yourself, speak to someone today: a doctor, a pastor, a trusted friend, or a crisis line in your country. If you are in danger right now, call your local emergency number. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Job asked for a little comfort before the end. Ask what small comfort you could bring to someone who feels their days are few. And ask whether your own fears about God sound more like Job's suffering talking than like what God has said.
